script.opening: "I’m a bit worried about Finn — for the last few months he keeps blinking a lot, scrunching his face, shrugging his shoulders, and making these throat-clearing and sniffing noises. He says he can hold them in for a bit but then has to do them. It’s worse when he’s tired or excited. Is it just a habit, or is it something serious like Tourette’s?"

facts.text: Mum, Sarah, with Finn (9) beside her. Finn blinks and clears his throat a few times during the call.

Started about 5 months ago with blinking, then face-scrunching, shoulder shrugs, throat-clearing and sniffing. Come and go; the type changes over weeks. Worse when tired, excited or watching screens; almost stop when he concentrates on Lego or football.
"Like an itch I have to scratch. If I do it, it goes away." Can hold them in at school for a while but "they come out more at home".
No jerks during sleep, no loss of awareness, no weakness. No recent sore throat or illness before they started. Development normal; no regression. No swearing tics. No medicines.

Doing fine at school; teacher hasn’t mentioned concentration problems. Not hyperactive. Likes things "just so" but no rituals that take up time. A bit anxious about tests. One boy copied his blinking last week; Finn was upset.
Dad "blinked a lot as a boy" and grew out of it. No family history of epilepsy.

Sarah: worried, tends to tell Finn to stop. Fears Tourette’s means swearing ("only what’s on TV"). Relieved by a calm explanation. Asks "So is it Tourette’s?" and "What should I do when he’s doing them?". Finn: shy, answers if spoken to directly.

ice.ideas: Sarah: "Either a habit he could stop, or Tourette’s."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she fears Tourette’s means shouting and swearing and that he’ll be bullied. Finn worries about being laughed at.
ice.expectations: "To know what it is, and whether I should be doing something — maybe a referral."

cues: "He can hold them in for a bit" — suppressible tics with a premonitory urge.
"Something serious like Tourette’s?" — fear to address with accurate information.
"A boy copied his blinking" (if school is asked) — impact and teasing.

checkpoints.text: Recognises TICS — sudden, repetitive, stereotyped motor/vocal movements that wax and wane, are briefly suppressible, worse with stress/tiredness, and often urge-preceded

Knows that tics are common and often transient/self-limiting, and the TOURETTE criteria (multiple motor tics + ≥1 vocal tic for >1 year, onset before 18) — recognising that a few months of tics is a provisional tic disorder — with most improving over time
Assesses IMPACT (school/social/self-esteem/bullying/physical) and screens the common COMORBIDITIES (ADHD, OCD, anxiety) that often matter more than the tics
REASSURES and gives psychoeducation (premonitory urge/suppressibility, that drawing attention worsens tics, managing stress/tiredness) — reassurance/education sufficient for mild tics

Refers/treats proportionately — behavioural therapy (habit-reversal/CBIT or exposure with response prevention) first-line, medication (specialist; aripiprazole usual first choice, ESSTS 2021, international) for severe tics — and considers RED FLAGS (sudden severe onset, neurological signs, developmental regression, very disabling tics)
Addresses the parent’s fear ("is it Tourette’s/serious?") with proportionate reassurance, validates concern, and explains sensitively
Gives practical psychoeducation and checks understanding, avoiding over-medicalising a common, often benign condition

Safety-nets and follows up: review if tics become impairing or comorbidities emerge, behavioural-therapy/specialist referral if needed, red flags warranting referral, and reassurance — proportionate, not over-medicalised, care

worked.txt: "What you’re describing are tics — the blinking, face-scrunching, shrugging and throat-clearing, that he can briefly hold in and that come and go and worsen when he’s tired or excited. They’re very common in children, and the reassuring news is most are mild and improve over time, often by the late teens."

"‘Tourette’s’ specifically means lots of movement tics plus at least one sound tic lasting over a year. Finn has had them for a few months, so it’s too early to say — at the moment we’d call it a tic disorder. Even if Finn meets that later, it’s not dangerous and it’s manageable — it doesn’t damage the brain."

"How are the tics affecting him — at school, with friends, any teasing? And a few related things often go alongside tics — trouble concentrating, anxiety, or repetitive worries/rituals. Any of those? Those can matter more than the tics themselves."
"A helpful tip: try not to keep telling him to stop — drawing attention to tics tends to make them worse. Reducing stress and tiredness helps, and the urge-then-tic pattern is normal."

"If the tics start really bothering him or getting in the way, there are effective behavioural therapies — habit-reversal training or exposure with response prevention — and the specialists can help, including medication for severe cases. We don’t need that for mild tics."

"Come back if the tics become distressing or disabling, if the concentration/anxiety side becomes a problem, or if anything changes suddenly or he loses skills — then I’d refer. Otherwise, reassurance and keeping an eye on it."

f.learning: TICS are sudden, repetitive, stereotyped MOTOR (blinking, grimacing, shrugging) or VOCAL (throat-clearing, sniffing, grunting) movements/sounds that characteristically WAX AND WANE, are briefly SUPPRESSIBLE, are worse with stress/excitement/tiredness, and are often preceded by a PREMONITORY URGE. Tics are COMMON in children and often TRANSIENT/self-limiting; TOURETTE SYNDROME is diagnosed when there are multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic for more than a year with onset before 18 (tics for under a year are a provisional tic disorder, as for Finn after a few months) — but many tic disorders are milder/transient, don’t meet Tourette criteria, and most improve over time (often by late adolescence). Assess the IMPACT (school, social situations, self-esteem, bullying, physical discomfort) and screen the common COMORBIDITIES — ADHD, OCD and anxiety (and learning difficulties) — which often matter more than the tics themselves. Reassure (tics are common, usually not a sign of serious underlying disease, and most are mild and improve) and give psychoeducation: explain the premonitory urge and suppressibility, that drawing attention to or criticising tics can worsen them, and that managing stress/tiredness helps — for mild tics, reassurance and education are often sufficient. Refer/treat proportionately if tics are significantly impairing or comorbidities need treatment: behavioural therapy — habit-reversal training / Comprehensive Behavioural Intervention for Tics (CBIT) or exposure with response prevention — is first-line (ESSTS European clinical guidelines 2021, international), with medication specialist-only for severe tics (aripiprazole usually first choice; clonidine where ADHD co-exists; BNFC), ADHD and OCD managed per NICE NG87 and NICE CG31, school support via the SENCo (Equality Act 2010, SEND Code of Practice), and consider red flags warranting referral (sudden severe onset, abnormal neurological signs — checked face to face — developmental regression, non-tic movements, very disabling tics). The skill is recognising tics/Tourette’s, reassuring appropriately, screening impact and comorbidities, and referring proportionately — not over-medicalising a common, often benign condition.

knowledge.guideline: [1] European clinical guidelines for Tourette syndrome and other tic disorders, version 2.0 (European Society for the Study of Tourette Syndrome, 2021) (international) · [2] NICE NG87 (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, 2018) · [3] NICE CG31 (obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder, 2005) · [4] BNFC (specialist-initiated medicines for tics) · [5] Equality Act 2010 and the SEND Code of Practice (2015)
knowledge.summary: Blinking, grimacing and shrugging with throat-clearing and sniffing, which come and go, are briefly suppressible, follow an urge and worsen with tiredness or excitement, are tics. Tics are common in children and usually mild. Tourette syndrome means several motor tics and at least one vocal tic for more than a year, starting in childhood. After a few months Finn does not yet meet that definition. The GP’s job is to recognise tics, check for red flags, ask about impact and common co-occurring conditions (ADHD, OCD, anxiety), reassure with good information, and refer only if tics are impairing or something else needs help.

points.t: Sudden, rapid, repeated movements or sounds. Simple motor tics: blinking, grimacing, shrugging. Simple vocal tics: sniffing, throat-clearing, grunting. They wax and wane, change over time, can be held back briefly at the cost of a building urge, and worsen with stress, excitement and tiredness. They often lessen during focused activity.

points.h: Tourette syndrome and other tic disorders
points.t: Tourette syndrome: multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic, present for more than a year, starting before 18. Tics lasting less than a year are a provisional (transient) tic disorder. Only a small minority have coprolalia. Tics usually peak around 10 to 12 years and lessen in the late teens for most.

Sudden explosive onset, loss of skills, abnormal neurological signs, movements that are not typical tics (such as chorea, or staring spells that could be absences), self-injurious tics, or severe distress. These need paediatric assessment.

points.h: Look for what comes with tics
points.t: ADHD, OCD, anxiety, learning difficulties, sleep problems and low mood are common and often cause more difficulty than the tics. Ask about concentration, worries, repeated rituals and school. ADHD and OCD have their own guidance (NICE NG87 [2], NICE CG31 [3]).

Explain what tics are and that they are not deliberate. Advise family and school not to comment on or tell him off for tics, which tends to make them worse. Good sleep and managing stress help. Written information and school awareness are part of treatment [1].

points.h: When to refer and what helps
points.t: If tics cause distress, pain, social or school problems, refer (paediatrics or CAMHS, per local pathway) for behavioural therapy: habit reversal training or CBIT, and exposure with response prevention are first-line [1]. Medication is specialist-only, for severe tics; aripiprazole is the usual first choice, with clonidine considered where ADHD co-exists [1, 4].

If tics or co-occurring conditions affect learning, the school’s SENCo can put support in place. A long-term tic disorder can meet the definition of disability under the Equality Act 2010 [5]. Watch for bullying.

dg.d: Open question to both; let the mother describe the tics fully and asked Finn about the urge in his own words.
Explored school, the worry about teasing (asked Finn directly), and his sleep.
Observed the tics and did a focused neurological examination; no tests needed.
Tics versus other movement disorders (chorea, myoclonus), absences and compulsions; provisional tic disorder versus Tourette syndrome.
Checked for sudden onset, regression, neurological signs and staring spells.
Provisional tic disorder, with motor and vocal tics for a few months; Tourette syndrome only if they persist beyond a year.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Psychoeducation, avoid drawing attention, sleep and stress, written information for school; no medication; habit reversal training if impairing.
Screened ADHD, OCD and anxiety; planned for teasing; involved school.
Return for worsening, pain, regression, distress or co-occurring problems; review in about three months.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the premonitory urge, suppressibility and improvement with focus as typical of tics, and the fear of Tourette’s from TV.
Idea: habit or Tourette’s. Concern: that it will turn into swearing and shouting; teasing. Expectation: to know what it is and what to do.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she fears Tourette’s means shouting and swearing and that he’ll be bullied. Finn worries about being laughed at — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Morgan. Hi Finn. What’s brought you both in today?
model.why: Greets the child and parent; open question

model.text: Mum: I’m a bit worried about Finn. For the last few months he keeps blinking a lot, scrunching his face, shrugging his shoulders, and making these throat-clearing and sniffing noises. He says he can hold them in for a bit but then has to do them. It’s worse when he’s tired or excited. Is it just a habit, or is it something serious like Tourette’s?
Thank you, that’s a really clear description. I’ll ask a few questions, including some for Finn, have a look at him, and then explain what I think. Is that okay?
Mum: Yes, please.
Finn, when you blink or clear your throat, what does it feel like just before?
model.why: Asks the child directly about the premonitory urge

model.text: Finn: Like an itch I have to scratch. If I do it, it goes away.
That’s a really good way to describe it. Mum, have the movements changed over the months, and does anything make them better?
model.why: Waxing and waning; relief with focus

model.text: Mum: They come and go. When he’s really concentrating on something, they almost stop.
Did they start suddenly, all at once, or gradually? And has he lost any skills, or had any clumsiness, weakness or odd staring spells?
Mum: Gradually. No, nothing like that. He’s doing fine otherwise.
How is school going, and has anyone said anything about the tics?
Mum: Fine, as far as I know. I just worry he’ll get teased.
Finn, is anyone unkind about it at school?
Finn: Not really.

Good. If that ever changes, tell your mum or your teacher. Some children with tics also find it hard to concentrate or sit still, or get lots of worries, or feel they have to do things in a certain way. Have you noticed anything like that?
Mum: Not that I’ve noticed.
And how is he sleeping?
Mum: Fine, mostly.
You mentioned Tourette’s. What do you know about it?
Mum: Only what’s on TV. People swearing and shouting. I’m scared that’s where it’s going.
That’s a very common worry. What are you hoping for from today?
Mum: To know what it is, and whether I should be doing something.
Can I watch Finn for a minute and do a quick check of his eyes, movements, coordination and walking?
Mum: Of course.

Everything I’ve examined is normal. What you’ve described are tics. The feeling before, being able to hold them in for a bit, getting better when he’s concentrating and worse when he’s tired, are all typical. Tics are very common in children his age, and most are mild and settle a lot by the late teens.
model.why: Names tics and reassures with specifics

model.text: Mum: So is it Tourette’s?

Tourette’s is a name we use when a child has several movement tics and at least one sound tic for more than a year. Finn’s have been there for a few months, so it’s too early to say. The swearing you see on TV is rare. And even if it did become Tourette’s, that’s not dangerous and doesn’t harm his brain or his intelligence.
model.why: Explains the criteria and addresses the specific fear

model.text: Mum: That’s a relief. What should I do when he’s doing them?

The most helpful thing is not to comment on them or ask him to stop. Drawing attention to tics usually makes them worse. Good sleep and keeping stress down help. I’ll give you some written information, and it would help to share it with his teacher.
Mum: And if he does get teased?

Then it’s worth speaking to his teacher. Schools can help classmates understand tics, and they should act on unkind behaviour. Finn, you’re not doing anything wrong. These are just something your body does.
model.why: Addresses bullying and speaks directly to the child

model.text: Finn: Okay.

At the moment the tics are mild and he’s coping, so there’s no need for medicine. If they start to bother him, hurt, or get in the way at school, there’s a helpful type of therapy called habit reversal training, which teaches him to manage the urge. I’d refer him then.
model.why: Proportionate plan with a clear threshold for referral

model.text: Mum: That makes sense.

Come back if the tics suddenly get much worse, cause pain or injury, if he loses any skills or seems unwell, if he’s very upset or struggling at school, or if concentration, worries or rituals start to cause problems. Can you tell me what you’ll do now?
Mum: Try not to mention them, get him sleeping well, talk to his teacher and share the leaflet. Come back if they get worse, cause problems, or anything changes.
Perfect. Let’s review in about three months to see how he’s getting on, or sooner if you need.

social.t: Copying and teasing can hurt self-esteem. School awareness sessions and a named contact help. Tics often lessen during absorbing activities, which children can use.
Parents often feel they should correct tics. Explaining why not to reduces family tension.

legal.t: A persistent tic disorder or Tourette syndrome can count as a disability. If it affects learning, the school’s SENCo can arrange support under the SEND Code of Practice.

professional.t: Involve Finn directly, in words he understands. Children describe the urge well and feel respected when asked.
Avoid over-medicalising mild tics, but refer promptly when tics or co-occurring conditions impair daily life.

community.t: Tourettes Action provides information for families and schools.

redFlags: Loss of skills or developmental regression
Abnormal neurological signs or staring spells
Self-injurious or painful tics; severe distress
psychosocial: School and the worry about teasing
Screen for anxiety, ADHD and OCD
ice: Expectation: to know what it is and what to do

playbook.diagnosis: Provisional tic disorder: several months of simple motor and vocal tics with a premonitory urge, brief suppressibility and waxing and waning, in a developmentally normal 9-year-old. No red flags. Tourette syndrome only if tics persist beyond a year.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “These are tics. They’re very common in children, they’re not his fault, and most get much better by the late teens. Tourette’s is only diagnosed when tics last more than a year, and even then it isn’t dangerous.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this was the start of the shouting and swearing you’ve seen on TV. That’s rare, and what Finn has at the moment is mild.”
management.psychosocial: Advice not to comment on tics; school involvement; plan for teasing; watch for anxiety.
sharedPlan: Explain tics; written information for family and school
Don’t draw attention to tics; good sleep; manage stress
Talk to the teacher about tic awareness and any teasing
Refer for habit reversal training or CBIT if impairing; medication only by a specialist
safetyNet: Return for sudden worsening, pain, regression or new neurological symptoms
Return if concentration, worries or rituals cause problems

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by either brushing tics off or over-treating them. The marks are for recognising them, calming the fear and seeing the whole child.

items.fail: Calling it a bad habit and telling him to stop.
items.why: Tics are involuntary; pressure makes them worse.

items.fail: Diagnosing Tourette’s at a few months.
items.why: The definition requires more than a year of tics.
items.fix: Say ‘tics’ now and explain when Tourette’s would apply.

items.why: They often cause more difficulty than the tics.
items.fix: Ask about concentration, worries and rituals.

items.why: Behavioural therapy is first-line; drugs are specialist-only.
items.fix: Psychoeducation now; habit reversal if impairing.

items.why: Finn can describe the urge and the teasing himself.
items.fix: Ask Finn directly and reassure him.

items.why: Sudden change or regression needs assessment.
items.fix: Give specific return reasons and a review date.

avoid.instead: “He can hold them in briefly, but it’s like holding in a sneeze. Please don’t comment on them.”
avoid.why: Pressure and attention make tics worse and blame the child.

avoid.instead: “They’re tics. Tourette’s means tics for more than a year, so it’s too early to say.”
avoid.why: The diagnosis needs at least a year of tics.

avoid.dont: “Let’s start a tablet to calm them.”
avoid.instead: “Mild tics don’t need medicine. If they start to cause problems, a behavioural therapy helps.”
avoid.why: Behavioural therapy is first-line; medication is specialist-only for severe tics (ESSTS 2021, international).

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Blinking, grimacing and shrugging with throat-clearing and sniffing, which come and go, are briefly suppressible, follow an urge and worsen with tiredness or excitement, are tics. Tics are common in children and usually mild. Tourette syndrome means several motor tics and at least one vocal tic for more than a year, starting in childhood. After a few months Finn does not yet meet that definition. The GP’s job is to recognise tics, check for red flags, ask about impact and common co-occurring conditions (ADHD, OCD, anxiety), reassure with good information, and refer only if tics are impairing or something else needs help.

points.t: Sudden, rapid, repeated movements or sounds. Simple motor tics: blinking, grimacing, shrugging. Simple vocal tics: sniffing, throat-clearing, grunting. They wax and wane, change over time, can be held back briefly at the cost of a building urge, and worsen with stress, excitement and tiredness. They often lessen during focused activity.

points.h: Tourette syndrome and other tic disorders
points.t: Tourette syndrome: multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic, present for more than a year, starting before 18. Tics lasting less than a year are a provisional (transient) tic disorder. Only a small minority have coprolalia. Tics usually peak around 10 to 12 years and lessen in the late teens for most.

Sudden explosive onset, loss of skills, abnormal neurological signs, movements that are not typical tics (such as chorea, or staring spells that could be absences), self-injurious tics, or severe distress. These need paediatric assessment.

points.h: Look for what comes with tics
points.t: ADHD, OCD, anxiety, learning difficulties, sleep problems and low mood are common and often cause more difficulty than the tics. Ask about concentration, worries, repeated rituals and school. ADHD and OCD have their own guidance (NICE NG87 [2], NICE CG31 [3]).

Explain what tics are and that they are not deliberate. Advise family and school not to comment on or tell him off for tics, which tends to make them worse. Good sleep and managing stress help. Written information and school awareness are part of treatment [1].

points.h: When to refer and what helps
points.t: If tics cause distress, pain, social or school problems, refer (paediatrics or CAMHS, per local pathway) for behavioural therapy: habit reversal training or CBIT, and exposure with response prevention are first-line [1]. Medication is specialist-only, for severe tics; aripiprazole is the usual first choice, with clonidine considered where ADHD co-exists [1, 4].

If tics or co-occurring conditions affect learning, the school’s SENCo can put support in place. A long-term tic disorder can meet the definition of disability under the Equality Act 2010 [5]. Watch for bullying.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question to both; let the mother describe the tics fully and asked Finn about the urge in his own words.
Explored school, the worry about teasing (asked Finn directly), and his sleep.
Picked up the premonitory urge, suppressibility and improvement with focus as typical of tics, and the fear of Tourette’s from TV.
Idea: habit or Tourette’s. Concern: that it will turn into swearing and shouting; teasing. Expectation: to know what it is and what to do.
Observed the tics and did a focused neurological examination; no tests needed.
Tics versus other movement disorders (chorea, myoclonus), absences and compulsions; provisional tic disorder versus Tourette syndrome.
Checked for sudden onset, regression, neurological signs and staring spells.
Provisional tic disorder, with motor and vocal tics for a few months; Tourette syndrome only if they persist beyond a year.
Psychoeducation, avoid drawing attention, sleep and stress, written information for school; no medication; habit reversal training if impairing.
Screened ADHD, OCD and anxiety; planned for teasing; involved school.
Return for worsening, pain, regression, distress or co-occurring problems; review in about three months.

social.t: Copying and teasing can hurt self-esteem. School awareness sessions and a named contact help. Tics often lessen during absorbing activities, which children can use.
Parents often feel they should correct tics. Explaining why not to reduces family tension.

legal.t: A persistent tic disorder or Tourette syndrome can count as a disability. If it affects learning, the school’s SENCo can arrange support under the SEND Code of Practice.

professional.t: Involve Finn directly, in words he understands. Children describe the urge well and feel respected when asked.
Avoid over-medicalising mild tics, but refer promptly when tics or co-occurring conditions impair daily life.

community.t: Tourettes Action provides information for families and schools.

redFlags: Loss of skills or developmental regression
Abnormal neurological signs or staring spells
Self-injurious or painful tics; severe distress
psychosocial: School and the worry about teasing
Screen for anxiety, ADHD and OCD
ice: Expectation: to know what it is and what to do

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Provisional tic disorder: several months of simple motor and vocal tics with a premonitory urge, brief suppressibility and waxing and waning, in a developmentally normal 9-year-old. No red flags. Tourette syndrome only if tics persist beyond a year.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “These are tics. They’re very common in children, they’re not his fault, and most get much better by the late teens. Tourette’s is only diagnosed when tics last more than a year, and even then it isn’t dangerous.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried this was the start of the shouting and swearing you’ve seen on TV. That’s rare, and what Finn has at the moment is mild.”
management.psychosocial: Advice not to comment on tics; school involvement; plan for teasing; watch for anxiety.
sharedPlan: Explain tics; written information for family and school
Don’t draw attention to tics; good sleep; manage stress
Talk to the teacher about tic awareness and any teasing
Refer for habit reversal training or CBIT if impairing; medication only by a specialist
safetyNet: Return for sudden worsening, pain, regression or new neurological symptoms
Return if concentration, worries or rituals cause problems

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by either brushing tics off or over-treating them. The marks are for recognising them, calming the fear and seeing the whole child.

items.fail: Calling it a bad habit and telling him to stop.
items.why: Tics are involuntary; pressure makes them worse.

items.fail: Diagnosing Tourette’s at a few months.
items.why: The definition requires more than a year of tics.
items.fix: Say ‘tics’ now and explain when Tourette’s would apply.

items.why: They often cause more difficulty than the tics.
items.fix: Ask about concentration, worries and rituals.

items.why: Behavioural therapy is first-line; drugs are specialist-only.
items.fix: Psychoeducation now; habit reversal if impairing.

items.why: Finn can describe the urge and the teasing himself.
items.fix: Ask Finn directly and reassure him.

items.why: Sudden change or regression needs assessment.
items.fix: Give specific return reasons and a review date.
